::: {#thm-walk-path}
#### A shortest walk is a path

Let $u$ and $v$ be vertices of a graph (@def-graph-vertices-edges) or a directed graph (@def-directed-graph).
If there is a walk (@def-walk) from $u$ to $v$, then every walk from $u$ to $v$ of the smallest possible length is a path (@def-graph-path).
In particular, there is then a path from $u$ to $v$.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

The lengths of the walks from $u$ to $v$, each plus 1, form a nonempty set of positive integers,
so that set has a smallest element (@rem-well-ordering),
and subtracting 1 from it gives the smallest length of a walk from $u$ to $v$.
Let $v_0, e_1, v_1, \ldots, e_n, v_n$ be a walk from $u$ to $v$ of that smallest length $n$.

Suppose, for contradiction (@def-proof-by-contradiction), that it is not a path.
Then $v_i = v_j$ for some $i < j$.
Leaving out the part between them gives the sequence

$$
v_0, e_1, \ldots, e_i, v_i, e_{j + 1}, v_{j + 1}, \ldots, e_n, v_n,
$$

which is still a walk from $u$ to $v$,
since the edge $e_{j + 1}$ joins $v_j = v_i$ to $v_{j + 1}$
(in a directed graph, it goes from $v_i$ to $v_{j + 1}$).
When $j = n$, the sequence ends at $v_i = v_n = v$.
Its length is $n - (j - i) < n$,
which contradicts the choice of $n$.
So the walk is a path.

:::

:::
